newsitem.title: UK: Polls point to North-South divide on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Polls point to North-South divide on EMU.

text.p: Southern Europeans and the French find the prospects of a single currency quite palatable, but the idea is more difficult to swallow in Germany and Britain, according to major polls published since the start of the year.

The common thread running through an array of surveys and polls carried out across the continent ahead of European economic and monetary union (EMU is that European citizens want a referendum on the issue before their governments commit to any formal plan.

In Germany and Britain in particular, citizens are keen to have their say, with 79 and 76 percent respectively for a referendum, a Gallup poll showed. Germany is widely held to be likely to lead the EMU launch group in January 1999, while Britain is expected to wait until the next century.

Analysts said a referendum in Germany was not an option. Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said he would be opposed, but the main political parties in Britain, scrambling for votes ahead of an election, have both promised a plebiscite before taking Britain into a single currency.
An ICM survey revealed 65 percent of Britons felt they were poorly informed about EMU.

"The ordinary British person has not had the arguments properly exposed to him primarily because of the complicated political situation," said John Arrowsmith, senior research fellow at the National Institute for Economic and Social Research (NIESR) in London.

Research by Groupe IFOP in France and DOXA in Italy showed that more than half the citizens in France and Italy would also welcome a say in the EMU process. Neither country has yet unveiled such plans.
In Portugal 76 percent of top politicians, civil servants and business people said they wanted a referendum.

But some analysts question the validity of asking citizens if they want a referendum. "It's like asking if they want lower taxes. They're bound to say yes," said Holger Schmeiding, senior economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
If European citizens did find themselves with a decision on their hands, referendum results could be quite different across borders.
The Italian government, hammering on the door to the EMU club, would find their efforts strongly backed by the population, with 71 percent likely to vote yes to a single currency, one survey showed.

In France, the results were less clear cut. Most recent survey findings have put support for EMU among citizens at between 56 and 61 percent, although a SOFRES survey said only 45 percent would be in favour.
But Germany, who along with France has steamrollered the process through, could face stiff opposition from a population wondering what's in it for them.
"Why would the Germans want to give up the mark, one of the best currencies in the world?" said Schmeiding.
Germany is worried that it may have to surrender the strong mark to a euro weakened by the lira, and that may cause problems for Kohl at the next election in 1998.
"EMU will not be a vote-winner for him," added Schmeiding.

In the Gallup survey, 44 percent of Germans said they would vote against a single currency. And an INRA institute poll at the end of 1996 showed that over half the population thought the euro could only be harmful to Germany.
Britain remains the most euro-sceptic. Recent surveys have shown that more than half of the population would vote against a single currency if given the chance.
Polls show that Sweden is unlikely to take the plunge in January 1999. But more than two-thirds of Finnish firms in a survey said Finland should be in the first wave.
